q.t: In 4/4, how many slots does the strum grid have per bar (counting 1 & 2 & …)?
q.e: 4 beats × 2 (number and &) = 8.

q.t: On which slots does the hand move down?
q.e: Down on numbers, up on &s — always.

q.t: In a strum grid, what does a dot (.) mean?
o: The hand moves but misses the strings
q.e: The hand keeps swinging; it just doesn't touch.

q.t: What is the 'everyday strum'?
An accent (>) means…
q.e: Accents are the strums you hit harder.

q.t: The backbeat is on beats…
q.e: The snare drum in rock and pop lands on 2 and 4.

q.t: What does PM mean?
q.e: Rest the side of the picking hand on the strings by the bridge.

q.t: What is a 'chuck'?
o: A dry percussive strum on muted strings
q.e: Fretting fingers lie lightly on the strings — strum gives a 'chk' like a snare.

q.t: Which strum fits 3/4 time?
q.e: Only 3 beats (6 slots): 1, 2 &, 3 &.

q.t: What's the first step to learn a new pattern?
o: Say it while clapping the beat
q.e: Say it, then mute and strum, then add one chord, then the changes.

q.t: Why does the hand keep moving on missed strums?
q.e: A hand that never stops is a clock: each strum lands in the right place.

q.t: In the everyday strum, which beat is missed?
q.e: ↓ . ↓ ↑ . ↑ ↓ ↑ — the down on 3 is skipped.

q.t: Missing a strong beat and playing around it is called…
q.e: Syncopation — the surprise makes the rhythm dance.

q.t: Why are up-strums usually lighter?
o: They catch only the top 3–4 strings
They are on the bass strings
q.e: Strong downs + light ups = bounce.

q.t: Why accent beats 2 and 4 in rock?
o: To lock in with the snare drum
q.e: The backbeat matches the snare, and it balances the naturally strong beat 1.

q.t: Why mute the strings when first learning a pattern?
o: So you focus only on rhythm
Muted strings are easier to tune
q.e: Taking chords away leaves just one thing to learn: the rhythm.

q.t: Why does palm muting sound 'chunky'?
o: The palm stops ringing and soaks up high overtones
q.e: Short, low, punchy notes — the rock rhythm sound.

q.t: Palm-muted power chord chugs are usually played with…
q.e: Downs hit the low strings harder and more evenly.

q.t: How many bars of the everyday strum fit in one cycle of Keherwa (8 beats)?
q.e: Keherwa = 8 beats = two bars of 4/4.

q.t: Your palm mute gives a dead thud with no note. What should you do?
o: Slide the palm back toward the bridge
q.e: Too far onto the strings kills the pitch. Move back until the note just comes through.

q.t: Write the everyday strum on the 8-slot grid (1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &).
q.e: Down, down-up, (miss) up-down-up.

q.t: Pattern ↓ . ↓ ↑ ↓ . ↓ ↑ has how many strums that touch the strings?
q.e: Two dots out of 8 slots, so 6 strums.

q.t: The everyday strum (↓ . ↓ ↑ . ↑ ↓ ↑) has how many up-strums?
In the everyday strum, the 'up' just after the missed beat 3 is on…
A 3/4 waltz strum has how many slots per bar?
q.e: 3 beats × 2 = 6.

q.t: Where do chucks usually go?
q.e: A chuck on 2 and 4 plays the backbeat — the guitar becomes the drum.

q.t: What do your fretting fingers do for a chuck?
o: Lie lightly on the strings without pressing
q.e: Light touch mutes the strings, so the strum is a dry 'chk'.

q.t: Why does every pattern fit the same down-up grid?
o: The hand is a pendulum: down on numbers, up on &s
All songs use the same pattern
Up-strums are not allowed on numbers
q.e: Once the motion is automatic, a new pattern is just a new choice of where to touch.

q.t: Why does starting at 60 BPM and adding 5 at a time work?
o: Fingers learn what is repeated correctly
60 BPM is the only real tempo
q.e: Repeat it right slowly; speed comes from accurate repetition.

q.t: You speed up the everyday strum but it keeps falling apart on beat 3. Best fix?
o: Slow down 5 BPM and keep the hand swinging
q.e: The hand must keep swinging through the miss; go slower until it's steady.

q.t: At 80 BPM in 4/4, how many strum-grid slots pass in one minute?
q.e: 80 beats × 2 slots = 160.

q.t: At 60 BPM, how long is one slot of the 8-slot grid?
q.e: One beat = 1 s; each beat has 2 slots, so ½ s each.

q.t: Which pattern has a strum on every slot?
q.e: All 8 slots touched — straight eighth notes.

q.t: In ↓ . x ↑ ↓ . x ↑, what happens on beats 2 and 4?
q.e: x = chuck, landing on the backbeat.

q.t: Which pattern is the same as the Week 4 'down, down-up'?
Why are palm-muted chugs sometimes switched to down-up at high speed?
o: All-downs can't keep up when it's very fast
q.e: Downs give the heaviest sound, but alternate picking doubles how fast you can go.

q.t: A pattern has accents on the & slots instead of the numbers. What effect does that have?
o: It sounds exactly like the backbeat
q.e: Stressing between the beats is syncopation — a jumpy, off-beat feel.

q.t: In the everyday strum, how many down-strums touch the strings?
q.e: Beats 1, 2 and 4 (beat 3 is missed).

q.t: You play the waltz strum (↓ . ↓ ↑ ↓ ↑) at 90 BPM. How many seconds is one bar?
q.e: 3 beats × (60 ÷ 90) s = 3 × ⅔ = 2 seconds.

q.t: Why is syncopation exciting to listen to?
o: It breaks the expected pattern, so the off-beats stand out
q.e: Your ear expects strong beats; when one is skipped, the notes around it pop out.
